rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Heading grammar is the mood switch, and it is load-bearing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: This is a lecture, so headings should default to claims. Three of four do: 'Durable state keeps the place', 'Feedback keeps the direction', and 'A boundary decides whether to continue' are each a declarative answer to their own implicit question. The fourth, l.29 'What stops a long-running session before done-done' (current wording), is the closest line in this file to tripping the rule -- it is phrased as a 'What X' construction rather than a claim, breaking the other three headers' own pattern, and the run->session vocabulary swap under review makes it echo the file's own H1 ('What keeps a long-running session going?') even more closely than before. It stays inside because the maintainer block names and defends exactly this inversion as deliberate: l.47 'The fourth slide (2026-08-14, Antti-directed) inverts the lecture's own frame, and its roster is a maintainer call. Three slides answer what keeps a run going; this one asks what ends it ahead of done-done...' -- that maintainer sentence is unchanged by the diff under review (only the heading and last bullet themselves were swapped, per the l.51 vocabulary accept-note), so the accept-note still applies to the current heading text. The interrogative form mirroring the H1 reads as intentional echo, not accidental drift, so the harm the rule guards against (mood confusion between instruction and stated law) is not present.
